Jacobus Arminius
j&-kō'būs ār-min'ī-ūs
n. (Jacobus Arminius, 1560–1609, Dutch minister and professor at Leiden whose teaching on conditional election provoked the controversy settled at Dort)
Latinized form of Dutch Jakob Harmenszoon; Jacobus, from Hebrew Ya'aqob, supplanter.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Jacobus Arminius was orphaned young, educated at Marburg, Leiden and Geneva under Beza, and settled as a preacher in Amsterdam before his 1603 appointment to the chair of theology at Leiden. He was by all accounts an able and gracious man; the dictionary does not quarrel with his manners but with his doctrine. Asked to refute a tract against predestination, he came instead to doubt the Reformed position, and taught that election is God's decree to save those whom He foresees will believe, that the atonement is universal in its intent, and that grace, though necessary, may be finally resisted. Each of those propositions reverses the direction of Scripture's own sentences. Rom 9:16 settles the question of origin: “So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy.” Act 13:48 settles the order: “as many as were ordained to eternal life believed.” John 6:44 settles the ability: “No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him.” Arminius died in 1609 before the storm broke; his followers drew up the Remonstrance the next year, and the Synod of Dort answered it in 1619.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines election as the choice of one or more from a greater number; and in theology, divine choice, or predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy.

expand to see more

ELEC'TION, n. The act of choosing; choice; the act of selecting one or more from others.

ELEC'TION, n. In theology, divine choice; predetermination of God, by which persons are distinguished as objects of mercy, become subjects of grace, are sanctified and prepared for heaven.

ARMIN'IAN, a. Pertaining to Arminius, or designating his principles.

Key Scripture

Rom 9:16 — "So then it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth, but of God that sheweth mercy."

Act 13:48 — "And when the Gentiles heard this, they were glad, and glorified the word of the Lord: and as many as were ordained to eternal life believed."

John 6:44 — "No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him: and I will raise him up at the last day."

Eph 1:4 — "According as he hath chosen us in him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before him in love:"

Modern Corruption

Arminianism is not a milder Calvinism but a different account of who saves whom; Dort answered it point for point and the answer still stands.

expand to see more

The error at the root is a reversal of order. Scripture makes faith the fruit of election; Arminius made election the acknowledgement of foreseen faith. Act 13:48 puts the ordaining first and the believing second, and Eph 1:4 puts the choosing before the foundation of the world, which is before there was any foreseen anything. Once the order is reversed the whole chain in Rom 8:30 loosens, for a predestination that waits upon man's decision cannot guarantee the calling, the justifying or the glorifying that the verse strings to it.

Modern evangelicalism has largely absorbed the Remonstrant position without knowing its name, and preaches a love of God that waits at the door of a will it dare not enter. That is not generosity toward sinners; it is a smaller gospel, because it leaves the decisive act in the hands of the dead. John 6:44 is the plain refutation: the Father draws, or no man comes. The Reformed answer honours God's mercy precisely by refusing to make it conditional upon the creature.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek eklegomai (G1586), to choose out; horizo (G3724), to mark out; helkuo (G1670), to draw.

expand to see more

Greek eklegomai (G1586) — to choose out for oneself; Ephesians 1:4.

Greek tasso (G5021) — to appoint, to ordain; Acts 13:48.

Greek helkuo (G1670) — to draw, to drag; John 6:44.

Greek eleeo (G1653) — to show mercy; Romans 9:16.

Greek proorizo (G4309) — to predestinate; Romans 8:30.

Usage

"“it is not of him that willeth, nor of him that runneth” (Rom 9:16) — the will is not the origin."

"“as many as were ordained to eternal life believed” (Act 13:48) — the ordaining comes first."

"“No man can come to me, except the Father which hath sent me draw him” (John 6:44) — the drawing is decisive."
